draft.title: Aboriginal knowledge of ecosystems
card: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have lived on and cared for Country for tens of thousands of years. Over that time they built detailed knowledge of plants, animals, seasons and the land.
This knowledge is passed on through stories, songs, art, ceremony and practice. It is held by communities and Elders, and it is part of living cultures today.
Fire management is one example. Cultural burning uses small, cool fires lit at chosen times and places, guided by knowledge of the local plants, animals and season.
Cultural burning can reduce fuel build-up and support the growth of some plants. Many land managers now work with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people to use this knowledge.
draft.remember: Long-held Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander knowledge of ecosystems, such as cultural burning, guides how land is cared for.

a.q: How is knowledge of ecosystems mainly passed on in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities?
opts: Through stories, songs, art and practice shared by Elders
Only through written reports from outside scientists
By each person working it out alone without teaching
Through a single record that no longer changes
a.why: The card explains that knowledge is passed on through stories, songs, art, ceremony and practice, and held by communities and Elders. It is a living knowledge, so it is not a single fixed record.
a.clue: Think about how Elders share knowledge with younger people.

b.q: A park ranger in Victoria works with a Traditional Owner group to plan a cultural burn. Why are the fires small and cool, and lit at chosen times and places?
opts: They follow local knowledge of plants, animals and season
They are lit at random times to copy lightning strikes
They aim to clear all plants so new land is made ready
They are lit only to make a path through the bush
b.why: Cultural burning is guided by knowledge of the local plants, animals and season, so fires are planned for time and place. It does not aim to clear all plants, which is the tempting wrong idea, because the fires are small and cool.
b.clue: Think about what the planners know about Country.

a.best: Through stories, songs, art and practice shared by Elders

b.best: They follow local knowledge of plants, animals and season

a.q: Which statement about Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander knowledge of ecosystems is accurate?
opts: It has built up over generations and is still used today
It was recorded once in the past and has not changed since
It was mostly lost and is no longer used in caring for land
It covers stories and art but not plants, animals or land
a.why: The knowledge was built over tens of thousands of years and is part of living cultures today, and land managers now work with it. It is not fixed or lost, and it covers plants, animals, seasons and the land, not only stories and art.
a.clue: Think about how long the knowledge took to build and whether it is used now.

b.q: A park ranger in Victoria works with a Traditional Owner group to plan a cultural burn. Which plan best matches cultural burning?
opts: Small, cool fires timed to the local season and plants
Large, hot fires in summer to clear all the fuel at once
Small fires lit on any day of the year to save planning
Cool fires lit across the whole state on the same day
b.why: Cultural burning uses small, cool fires lit at chosen times and places, guided by the local plants, animals and season. A large, hot fire is tempting because it burns fuel, but it is not the small, cool, planned fire the card describes.
b.clue: Two things matter here: the size of the fire and how it is timed.
